props.title: It Started in Naples

sections.content: It Started in Naples (1960) represents a fascinating intersection of Hollywood glamour and Italian cinema's golden age. Clark Gable, in one of his final roles, brings his characteristic charm opposite the luminous Sophia Loren in this romantic comedy set against the stunning Amalfi Coast. The film follows a similar pattern to Roman Holiday (1953) and Three Coins in the Fountain (1954), where American characters discover love amid picturesque Italian landscapes. Director Melville Shavelson captures the vibrant energy of Naples, using its narrow streets, bustling markets, and Mediterranean vistas as more than just backdrop.

sections.content: The film's cultural clash narrative became a template for many subsequent Italian-American romantic comedies. Like Marriage Italian Style (1964) and Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow (1963), it explores the dynamic between American pragmatism and Italian passion. Sophia Loren's performance as Lucia Curcio showcases why she became Italy's most successful crossover star, combining dramatic depth with comic timing. The film's treatment of Naples' street life and its portrayal of young Marietto (played by Carlo Angeletti) influenced later works like Cinema Paradiso (1988) in their depiction of Italian childhood.

The technical achievements of It Started in Naples deserve special attention. Shot in Technicolor by cinematographer Robert Surtees, the film captures Naples in vivid hues that influenced later Italian productions like Purple Noon (1960) and L'Avventura (1960). The musical sequences, featuring Loren performing "Tu Vuò Fà L'Americano," demonstrate how Hollywood adapted Italian popular culture for international audiences. sections.content: The legacy of It Started in Naples extends beyond its immediate era. Its influence can be seen in later cross-cultural romances like Only You (1994) and Under the Tuscan Sun (2003), which continue to use Italy as a transformative setting for American characters. The film's approach to bilingual dialogue and cultural misunderstandings created a blueprint for international co-productions, while its portrayal of Naples helped establish the city as a viable location for international productions.
